summary: Defines two SIP header fields, Resource-Priority and Accept-Resource-Priority, for communicating resource priority. They can influence how SIP user agents, such as gateways and IP phones, and SIP proxies behave, but not how IP routers forward packets. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Some calls matter more, such as emergency ones. This lets a call carry a priority tag so phone gear knows which calls to take care of first.

questions: what does sip 417 unknown resource-priority mean
what is the dsn namespace in sip
subtitle: SIP header fields that mark a request as deserving priority access to scarce gateway, proxy and phone resources.

tldr.problem: During emergencies, telephone circuits, gateways and SIP proxies can become congested, and SIP had no way for a request to say that it should get prioritized access to them.
tldr.mechanism: The Resource-Priority header field carries one or more namespace.priority values, and Accept-Resource-Priority lists the values an element accepts. Elements that understand a value authorize the request, then preempt lower-priority sessions or queue the request.
tldr.outcome: Elements that do not understand the header ignore it, so it is backwards compatible. It does not change how IP routers forward packets. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 7134.

today: RFC 4412 is a Proposed Standard and is listed as updated by RFC 7134. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Calls Need Priority
sections.content:
In emergencies, communications resources such as telephone circuits, IP bandwidth and gateways between circuit-switched and IP networks may become congested. This RFC covers real-time applications that use SIP, including voice over IP, conferencing, instant messaging and presence. It names five scarce resources: gateways, circuit-switched network resources, IP network resources, receiving end systems and SIP proxies. IP network resources are outside the scope of SIP signaling.

SIP had no way for a request originator to ask for prioritized treatment, so the RFC adds a label for requests. This differs from the existing Priority header field in RFC 3261, which says how important a request is to the human receiver and does not affect PSTN gateway or proxy resources. Any caller can assert any Priority value, while use of Resource-Priority is subject to authorization.

The header does not directly influence IP router forwarding, though other documents may define procedures that do. SIP elements and user agents that act on the header are called RP actors.
sections.plainLanguage: When everyone calls at once, the lines jam. A priority label lets the important calls, like those of emergency helpers, get through first.

sections.title: The Two Header Fields
sections.content:
Resource-Priority is a request header. Each value is written namespace.priority, for example dsn.flash. Namespaces and priority values are case-insensitive ASCII tokens without periods, so dsn.flash and DSN.Flash are equivalent. They MUST be registered with IANA.

A request may carry values from several namespaces, because a call can cross administrations with different priority schemes and there is no global ordering among them. A particular namespace MUST NOT appear more than once in a message. Values can be in one comma-separated list or in several header fields, and their order has no meaning.

Accept-Resource-Priority is a response header listing the values a user agent server is willing to process. It does not promise that a call will find enough resources. Domains MAY hide it, but that is NOT RECOMMENDED because it helps troubleshooting.

The RFC also defines the resource-priority option tag, used in Require and Supported.
sections.plainLanguage: A priority sticker reads like a club name, a dot and a level. A second note says which stickers a phone will honor.

sections.title: How Elements Handle Prioritized Requests
sections.content:
An RP actor follows three steps. If it recognizes none of the namespaces, it treats the request as having no Resource-Priority header. Otherwise it checks that the request is authorized by local policy, and rejects it if not. If it is authorized and resources are available, it serves the request normally. If resources are short, the actor either preempts existing sessions or places the request in a priority queue.

With preemption, a higher-priority session may displace more than one lower-priority one, and requests do not preempt others of equal priority. Proxies do not manage sessions, so they do not preempt. A user agent that ends a session sends BYE with a Reason header, as described in RFC 4411.

With queueing, requests wait in first-come, first-served order within each priority, and the longest-waiting request in the highest non-empty queue is served first. A full queue rejects new requests at once. A wait-time limit can eject requests with 408 (Request Timeout), and a user agent server SHOULD send 182 (Queued) while waiting.

An OPTIONS request can be used to discover support. Responses MUST include Supported with the resource-priority tag. Proxies MAY ignore the header, and MAY upgrade, downgrade or insert it if local policy allows.
sections.plainLanguage: When a room is full, a very important guest can ask someone less important to leave, or wait in a line where the important guests are served first.

sections.title: When a Prioritized Request Fails
sections.content:
A request can fail for four reasons, each with its own response.

  • Unknown value: without Require: resource-priority, the request is processed at default priority and the unknown values MUST NOT be changed. With the option tag, the element MUST answer 417 (Unknown Resource-Priority), and MAY include Accept-Resource-Priority.
  • Not authenticated: 401 (Unauthorized) or 407 (Proxy Authentication Required).
  • Not authorized: 403 (Forbidden).
  • No resources: 503 (Service Unavailable) if signaling capacity is short, 488 (Not Acceptable Here) for missing media capacity, and 486 (Busy Here) when a phone is busy with equal or higher priority calls.

Treating unknown values as absent by default is needed so that a call can still complete when a proxy in the middle shares no namespace with the two endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: If the guard does not know your sticker, asks who you are, says you are not allowed, or finds the room full, each case has its own answer.

sections.title: Namespaces and Their Ordering
sections.content:
A single request may contain values from several namespaces. An actor ignores those it does not recognize. If it understands more than one, it MUST create a local total ordering over all of their values that keeps the relative order inside each namespace. The RFC recommends using the same ordering throughout an administrative domain.

The RFC registers five namespaces: dsn (Defense Switched Network, 5 levels, preemption), drsn (Defense RED Switched Network, 6 levels, preemption), q735 (5 levels, preemption), ets (Emergency Telecommunications Service, 5 levels, queue) and wps (Wireless Priority Service, 5 levels, queue).

The DSN levels, lowest to highest, are routine, priority, immediate, flash and flash-override. DRSN adds flash-override-override, which displaces another request of equal priority. The q735, ets and wps levels run from 4 (lowest) to 0 (highest). New namespaces MUST be defined in a Standards Track RFC and list a finite set of levels.
sections.plainLanguage: Different groups use different sticker systems. A phone that knows two of them just makes one big ranked list, keeping each group's own order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any resource priority mechanism can be abused to take resources and deny service to others. An adversary might take over a PSTN gateway or end existing calls on an IP phone. Requests with this header are therefore likely to have stricter authentication than ordinary ones, including for users inside the same domain.

All user agents and proxies that support the extension MUST implement SIP over TLS, the sips URI scheme and Digest authentication. User agents SHOULD also implement S/MIME. If S/MIME protects the message, the header must also appear in the outer message for proxies to act on it. Third parties can vouch for the requester through authenticated identity or asserted identity.

The RFC expects deliberate denial-of-service attacks during emergencies, and says systems should minimize state, computation and network resources an unauthorized user can command.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the sticker gives a big advantage, people will try to fake it. So the system has to check carefully who is allowed to use it.
